books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Abraham Lincoln, speech to the Illinois Republican State Convention, Springfield, June 16, 1858

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, speech to the Illinois Republican State Convention, Springfield, June 16, 1858; public domain.
stimulus.text:
“We are now far into the fifth year, since a policy was initiated, with the avowed object, and confident promise, of putting an end to slavery agitation. Under the operation of that policy, that agitation has not only, not ceased, but has constantly augmented. In my opinion, it will not cease, until a crisis shall have been reached, and passed — “A house divided against itself cannot stand.” I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free. I do not expect the Union to be dissolved — I do not expect the house to fall — but I do expect it will cease to be divided. It will become all one thing, or all the other.”
— Abraham Lincoln, speech to the Illinois Republican State Convention, Springfield, June 16, 1858

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from Abraham Lincoln, “House Divided” speech (1858), public domain
stem: By 1877, in what way had Lincoln’s prediction that the house would “cease to be divided” come true, and in what way had it not?

options.text: It had come true because the South had rejoined the Union as slave states, and it had not because the North refused to accept them.
options.misconception: The South rejoined without slavery; the 13th Amendment had abolished it in 1865.

options.text: It had come true because the federal government had given up all power over the states, and it had not because the states still quarreled over tariffs.
options.misconception: The federal government grew stronger, not weaker, and tariffs were not the division Lincoln named.

options.text: It had come true because the Southern states had all accepted Black equality, and it had not because Northern states still allowed slavery.
options.misconception: Southern states resisted Black equality with Black Codes and terror, and no Northern state still allowed slavery.

options.text: It had come true because the 13th Amendment made the whole nation free territory, and it had not because Black Americans’ new rights were already being hollowed out.

rationales.A: The 13th Amendment abolished slavery in 1865, so no state rejoined as a slave state.
rationales.B: The war and the amendments strengthened federal power, and Lincoln’s division was about slavery, not tariffs.
rationales.C: The Southern states did not accept Black equality, and slavery was gone in the North long before 1877.
rationales.D: The half-slave, half-free division Lincoln named was gone: slavery was abolished everywhere in 1865. Background: yet the books and the period review show the promise of the 14th and 15th Amendments met Black Codes, the Ku Klux Klan, and the Compromise of 1877, which pulled federal troops out of the South.
rationales.general:
1. Take the first half. Lincoln said the house would cease to be divided, and the 13th Amendment abolished slavery everywhere in 1865.
2. Take the second half. The 14th and 15th Amendments promised citizenship and the vote, but Black Codes, the Ku Klux Klan, and the Compromise of 1877 hollowed those promises out.
3. Hold both halves at once. The legal division over slavery ended, while the fight over Black rights went on.
4. Name the pattern. A war can settle one question and leave the next one open.
Remember: when a prediction comes half true, say exactly which half came true and which did not.
